sweep_summary: Southeast Ijo (Nembe) is not in the catalog. Both title-works with stress in the title are unpublished University of Port Harcourt theses on Nembe pitch accent (Ikoko 2003 MA, 110 pp; Efere 1981, actually a B.A. long essay comparing Bumo [Izon] and Nembe); Second-hand traces: Faraclas 1984 cites Efere 1981 for four noun pitch classes assigned over a pitch phrase, and Williamson 1988 states its Bumo analysis rests on Efere 1981. The best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Williamson 1988 sec. 2.3 (already held by the project): Nembe is a pitch accent lect with class-determined prelinked H (none for Class A, final for merged B/C, non-final for merged D/E), default L elsewhere, no domain tones — i.e. lexical accent, no fixed stress. Acquisition priority: Ikoko 2003 high (the only dedicated monograph-length study), Efere 1981 medium. Trace file and entry

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nembe is analysed as a pitch accent (reduced two-tone H/L) system, not a stress system: the 'accent' is a lexically prelinked H tone whose location is a property of the morpheme's lexical class — class B=C morphemes carry the H on their final syllable, class D=E morphemes carry one or more H's with a single H never on the final syllable, and class A morphemes have no linked H at all (only a floating H that is placed by rule on or next to a following enclitic, else deleted). There are no spreading (domain) tones; syllables preceding the linked H receive default L. Accent position is therefore lexical/morphological, not fixed on any syllable counted from a word edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the framework has only H placement (prelinked/floating) plus default L — no secondary prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics carry their own floating H with a complex placement rule (deleted after a linked H; realised on the enclitic or on the preceding syllable depending on context — 'FTPlace is considerably more complex in Nembe than in Kolokuma or in Kalabari'); group-initial V-syllables may behave differently from CV-syllables (sec. 1.2).
new_statements.domain_note: The domain is the syntactically defined 'group' (object+verb, noun with its preceding modifiers, etc.): 'The pitch pattern of a group is chiefly, in many cases entirely, determined by the class of the initial morpheme.. a group can be conceived as having a prosodic structure in which the first morpheme is strong and the others weak' (p. 254-255); non-initial morphemes lose their tones. Isolation forms in Table 1 (dialect 42 NE): Class A LL, Classes B and C LH.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1988 describes the Nembe dialect (Glottolog nemb1238) of Southeast Ijo, using data from Rowlands 1960 and Efere 1981; Akassa/Akaha (akas1241) is not separately analysed there, but Williamson & Blench (2009, ELL2 'Ijo') state that 'Nembe-Akaha' as a whole has a pitch accent system. In Williamson's Table 1 Nembe is dialect no. 42 (NE) and Akassa presumably 41, i.e. within her range '321-42.. pitch accent systems'.

new_statements.reading: Nembe (Southeast Ijo, Williamson's dialect 42 NE, classed with dialects 321-42 as 'pitch accent systems') has no stress in the intensity sense and no fixed positional accent: word prosody is a lexical pitch accent realised as a 'prelinked H' whose position is fixed per lexical class — Class A morphemes carry no prelinked H (all-low in isolation, e.g. LL 'town'), the merged Classes B/C carry it on the final syllable (LH), the merged Classes D/E carry one or more prelinked Hs which, if single, is never on the final syllable; syllables before the accent take default L, and there are no domain (spreading) tones. The accent domain is the syntactic 'group', whose pitch is set by its initial morpheme. So accent placement is lexically contrastive (class-determined), not phonologically predictable. This is first-hand analysis by Williamson (building on Rowlands 1960 for Nembe), already held by the project from our earlier reading and read in this search of works with stress in the title; it is not one of the two works with stress in the title.
